course.title: Visual Course Volume 6 - Durable Orchestration and Multi-Agent Workflows
course.subtitle: Coordinate long-running work that survives retries, restarts, people, and partial failure
course.audience: A visual learner who understands protocols and knowledge systems and now wants to coordinate reliable work across queues, workers, specialist agents, approvals, and external systems

knowledgeBaseline.state: Conversation, run, task, and workflow state are different records with different lifetimes
knowledgeBaseline.durability: Business progress is reconstructed from durable history and artifacts, not trusted to one process's memory
knowledgeBaseline.delivery: Duplicate delivery is normal, so side-effecting workers need idempotency and durable receipts
knowledgeBaseline.coordination: Orchestration and choreography are design choices; neither removes partial failure
knowledgeBaseline.control: Budgets, approvals, cancellation, and final authority are explicit workflow contracts
knowledgeBaseline.recovery: Chaos tests and recovery drills prove that incomplete work can be found and safely resumed

lessons.title: Conversation state, run state, task state, and workflow state
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show four separate layers labeled CONVERSATION, AGENT RUN, A2A TASK, BUSINESS WORKFLOW. Give each a different ID, OWNER, LIFETIME, and STORE. Use dashed CORRELATION ID links across layers. A coral MERGED SESSION STORE collapses all four and is labeled LOST OWNERSHIP.
lessons.alt: Four distinct state layers for conversation, agent run, A2A task, and business workflow are correlated without being merged, while one combined session store is rejected.
lessons.outcome: Choose the correct state record and identity for a chat turn, model attempt, delegated task, or long-running business case.
lessons.explanation: A conversation remembers what people said. An agent run records one attempt to decide or act. An A2A task represents stateful work exchanged between agents. A business workflow owns the real case from start to final outcome, even across many conversations and runs. The important beginner move is to treat the lifetime and owner of each state layer as an explicit contract, not as hidden framework behavior. The safety rule is: closing a browser tab or retrying a model run must not erase or duplicate the business case. The durable record must say what was requested, which identity owns it, what changed, which attempt produced the change, and what may legally happen next. Frameworks can store and replay that record in different ways, but a restart must never change the business meaning. Keep protocol messages, queue delivery, model reasoning, and business truth separate: a transport can retry, a worker can disappear, and an agent can revise its proposal while the authoritative workflow record remains inspectable.

A task ID tracks delegated work, status, messages, and artifacts.
A workflow ID owns business progress, approvals, side effects, and receipts.
Correlation IDs connect the layers without pretending that they are one record.
lessons.analogy: It is like a hospital visit: the conversation is what you say, the test run is one examination, the referral is a specialist task, and the patient case is the durable medical journey.

lessons.diagramPrompt: Show USER COMMAND entering VALIDATE INVARIANTS. Valid path emits an EVENT into APPEND-ONLY HISTORY and a reducer moves STATE from OPEN to WAITING APPROVAL. Coral invalid path emits COMMAND REJECTED and leaves state unchanged. Labels: COMMAND, INVARIANT, EVENT, STATE.
lessons.alt: A command is checked against invariants, accepted as an event that changes state, or rejected without changing state.
lessons.outcome: Model workflow change as commands checked by rules, facts recorded as events, and legal states derived from those facts.
lessons.explanation: A command asks for something to happen; it may be refused. An event states that something did happen; history should not rewrite it. A state machine lists the legal states and transitions. Invariants are rules that must remain true before and after every accepted transition. The important beginner move is to treat the line between requested intent and recorded fact as an explicit contract, not as hidden framework behavior. The safety rule is: a refund cannot move to completed unless approval and payment evidence already exist. The durable record must say what was requested, which identity owns it, what changed, which attempt produced the change, and what may legally happen next. Frameworks can store and replay that record in different ways, but a restart must never change the business meaning. Keep protocol messages, queue delivery, model reasoning, and business truth separate: a transport can retry, a worker can disappear, and an agent can revise its proposal while the authoritative workflow record remains inspectable.

lessons.analogy: A command is asking a referee to award a goal; the event is the referee recording it; the scoreboard is the derived state.

lessons.title: Checkpoints, snapshots, replay, and schema evolution
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show APPEND-ONLY EVENTS 1 TO 900 flowing into SNAPSHOT AT 800, then REPLAY 801 TO 900 to rebuild CURRENT STATE. Above, CODE V1 and CODE V2 cross a VERSION GATE. Coral INCOMPATIBLE EVENT goes to MIGRATION TEST. Include CONTINUE AS NEW as a clean-history branch.
lessons.alt: A snapshot plus later events rebuilds current state while code versions and migration tests protect replay compatibility, with a continue-as-new branch for long histories.
lessons.outcome: Recover workflow state quickly while preserving replay correctness as histories and code change.
lessons.explanation: An event history is the durable recipe for rebuilding progress. A snapshot is a performance shortcut that captures state at a known event, not a replacement for business evidence. Replay applies later events again. Because old histories may run against new code, workflow logic and event schemas need compatible evolution or explicit version gates. The important beginner move is to treat the compatibility boundary between stored history and deployed workflow code as an explicit contract, not as hidden framework behavior. The safety rule is: replaying the same accepted history must produce the same decisions and commands. The durable record must say what was requested, which identity owns it, what changed, which attempt produced the change, and what may legally happen next. Frameworks can store and replay that record in different ways, but a restart must never change the business meaning. Keep protocol messages, queue delivery, model reasoning, and business truth separate: a transport can retry, a worker can disappear, and an agent can revise its proposal while the authoritative workflow record remains inspectable.

Create a snapshot only after a known durable history position.
Restore the snapshot and replay only the later events.
Test old histories against candidate code before deployment.
Use version markers, migrations, or a new execution when history growth or incompatible change demands it.
lessons.analogy: It is like resuming a long book from a trustworthy bookmark while keeping the earlier chapters available for proof.

walkthrough: The old history includes the workflow version selected when the case began.

caseStudy.danger: Changing workflow code as if no old histories exist can cause nondeterministic replay or silently different decisions.
caseStudy.takeaway: History is an API consumed by future code; evolve it deliberately.

lessons.checkpoint: Does a snapshot replace the event history?
lessons.answer: No. It speeds restoration from a known point; the history and durable business records still explain what happened.
glossary: Replay - rebuilding progress from recorded events
Snapshot - state captured at a known history position
Schema evolution - changing stored contracts safely

A business record is the system-of-record fact used by the organization. These objects can refer to one another, but they are not interchangeable. The important beginner move is to treat the ownership and authority of each durable output as an explicit contract, not as hidden framework behavior. The safety rule is: a pleasant agent message must never be the only evidence that money moved or a case closed. The durable record must say what was requested, which identity owns it, what changed, which attempt produced the change, and what may legally happen next. Frameworks can store and replay that record in different ways, but a restart must never change the business meaning. Keep protocol messages, queue delivery, model reasoning, and business truth separate: a transport can retry, a worker can disappear, and an agent can revise its proposal while the authoritative workflow record remains inspectable.

lessons.title: Queues, workers, leases, acknowledgements, and visibility
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show PRODUCER to DURABLE QUEUE to WORKER A. Delivery creates a LEASE or VISIBILITY WINDOW. Success returns ACK and removes the item. A coral WORKER CRASH lets the lease expire and WORKER B receives the same item. Include RECEIPT before ACK.
lessons.alt: A queue leases work to a worker; success records a receipt and acknowledges it, while a crash lets the lease expire so another worker receives the same item.
lessons.outcome: Explain why a worker owns a delivery temporarily and why acknowledgement happens only after durable success.
lessons.explanation: A durable queue separates the producer's speed from the worker's speed. Receiving an item normally creates a temporary lease or visibility window, not permanent ownership. The worker finishes the durable result and then acknowledges. If it crashes first, the item becomes available again. The important beginner move is to treat the temporary ownership represented by the delivery lease as an explicit contract, not as hidden framework behavior. The safety rule is: a work item is acknowledged only after the result or receipt needed for recovery is durable. The durable record must say what was requested, which identity owns it, what changed, which attempt produced the change, and what may legally happen next. Frameworks can store and replay that record in different ways, but a restart must never change the business meaning. Keep protocol messages, queue delivery, model reasoning, and business truth separate: a transport can retry, a worker can disappear, and an agent can revise its proposal while the authoritative workflow record remains inspectable.
trace: The producer writes a small typed work envelope to a durable queue.
A worker receives it with a delivery identity and temporary lease.
The worker heartbeats or extends visibility only while it is genuinely progressing.
It commits its result and receipt before acknowledging the delivery.
A crash or expired lease causes redelivery to the same or another worker.
lessons.analogy: It is like taking a library book from the returns cart with a temporary claim ticket; if you vanish, someone else can finish shelving it.

lessons.title: Backpressure, rate limits, admission control, and priorities
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show REQUEST FLOOD entering ADMISSION GATE with CAPACITY, TENANT LIMIT, PRIORITY, and DEADLINE checks. Accepted work enters HIGH, NORMAL, BULK queues and sized WORKER POOLS. Coral OVERLOAD returns RETRY LATER. Teal CAPACITY SIGNAL flows backward.
lessons.alt: An admission gate uses capacity, tenant limits, priority, and deadlines to route accepted work into separate queues while overload returns a retry-later result and capacity signals flow upstream.
lessons.outcome: Protect workers and important users by limiting intake before a queue becomes an invisible failure reservoir.
lessons.explanation: Backpressure is the downstream system telling producers to slow down. Rate limits protect a boundary over time. Admission control decides whether new work should enter now. Priorities choose which accepted work goes first, but fairness prevents one urgent tenant from starving everyone else. The important beginner move is to treat the admission gate between demand and available capacity as an explicit contract, not as hidden framework behavior. The safety rule is: the system must reject or defer excess work before queues, budgets, and deadlines become unrecoverable. The durable record must say what was requested, which identity owns it, what changed, which attempt produced the change, and what may legally happen next. Frameworks can store and replay that record in different ways, but a restart must never change the business meaning. Keep protocol messages, queue delivery, model reasoning, and business truth separate: a transport can retry, a worker can disappear, and an agent can revise its proposal while the authoritative workflow record remains inspectable.

Classify work by tenant, risk, deadline, and service class.

Return an explicit retry-after, deferred status, or safe degradation when overloaded.
lessons.analogy: A restaurant controls seating at the door because filling every hallway with waiting diners does not create more cooks.

lessons.title: Retries, idempotency keys, deduplication, and poison work
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show WORK ITEM with IDEMPOTENCY KEY entering ATTEMPT 1 TIMEOUT then ATTEMPT 2. Both check DEDUP STORE. Existing RECEIPT returns SAME RESULT. Repeated deterministic failure goes to POISON or DEAD LETTER after RETRY BUDGET. No infinite loop.
lessons.alt: Retried attempts share an idempotency key and deduplication store so an existing receipt returns the same result, while repeated nonrecoverable failure moves to a poison-work lane.
lessons.outcome: Retry transient failure without repeating the intended business effect or trapping bad work in an infinite loop.
lessons.explanation: A retry creates another attempt, not another user intention. An idempotency key names that stable intention. The receiver stores the key with a request fingerprint, status, and result so the same request can return the same outcome. Poison work is repeatedly unprocessable because of bad data, incompatible code, or a permanent rule failure. The important beginner move is to treat the deduplication boundary around one intended side effect as an explicit contract, not as hidden framework behavior. The safety rule is: all attempts for one intention share one key, and the same key cannot be reused for a different request. The durable record must say what was requested, which identity owns it, what changed, which attempt produced the change, and what may legally happen next. Frameworks can store and replay that record in different ways, but a restart must never change the business meaning. Keep protocol messages, queue delivery, model reasoning, and business truth separate: a transport can retry, a worker can disappear, and an agent can revise its proposal while the authoritative workflow record remains inspectable.

lessons.analogy: It is like a numbered coat-check ticket: asking again with the same ticket retrieves the same coat, not a second coat.

lessons.title: Deadlines, cancellation, timeout, and compensation
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show WORKFLOW with absolute DEADLINE flowing into STEP A then STEP B. USER CANCEL sends cooperative CANCELLATION. A TIMER creates TIMEOUT. Completed reversible STEP A has coral COMPENSATE A path. IRREVERSIBLE STEP B has POINT OF NO RETURN and MANUAL RECOVERY.
lessons.alt: A workflow carries a deadline, responds cooperatively to cancellation and timeout, compensates a completed reversible step, and treats an irreversible step as a point of no return.
lessons.outcome: Distinguish a request to stop, a timer expiring, and business work required to repair completed effects.
lessons.explanation: A deadline is the latest useful completion time and should travel with the work. Cancellation is a request to stop; a worker may need a safe checkpoint before honoring it. A timeout is the system deciding that a wait exceeded its bound. Compensation is new business work that counteracts a completed effect; it is not a database rewind. The important beginner move is to treat the point where waiting ends but previously committed effects remain real as an explicit contract, not as hidden framework behavior. The safety rule is: after the point of no return, the workflow must finish forward or enter an explicit manual recovery state. The durable record must say what was requested, which identity owns it, what changed, which attempt produced the change, and what may legally happen next. Frameworks can store and replay that record in different ways, but a restart must never change the business meaning. Keep protocol messages, queue delivery, model reasoning, and business truth separate: a transport can retry, a worker can disappear, and an agent can revise its proposal while the authoritative workflow record remains inspectable.

Propagate cancellation to cancellable children and activities.

Expose cancelled, timed-out, compensated, and manual-recovery outcomes separately.
lessons.analogy: Stopping a cake recipe is easy before baking; after it is baked, you cannot unbake it, so recovery means a different action.

lessons.title: Orchestration versus choreography
lessons.diagramPrompt: Split canvas. Left ORCHESTRATION: one COORDINATOR sends COMMANDS to POLICY, FINANCE, NOTIFY and receives RESULTS. Right CHOREOGRAPHY: services publish FACT EVENTS through EVENT BUS and react independently. Bottom compares GLOBAL VIEW, COUPLING, RECOVERY, and OWNERSHIP.
lessons.alt: A side-by-side comparison shows a coordinator directing services in orchestration and services reacting to fact events through a bus in choreography, with ownership and recovery trade-offs.
lessons.outcome: Choose deliberate central coordination, event reactions, or a hybrid based on ownership and recovery needs.
lessons.explanation: In orchestration, one workflow decides which command comes next and owns the end-to-end state. In choreography, participants publish facts and other participants react without one controller knowing the full route. Orchestration makes global progress and recovery visible; choreography reduces central coupling but can hide the business journey across many reactions. The important beginner move is to treat the owner of the end-to-end business decision as an explicit contract, not as hidden framework behavior. The safety rule is: every cross-service business process still needs a discoverable owner and recovery policy even when no single runtime coordinates every step. The durable record must say what was requested, which identity owns it, what changed, which attempt produced the change, and what may legally happen next. Frameworks can store and replay that record in different ways, but a restart must never change the business meaning. Keep protocol messages, queue delivery, model reasoning, and business truth separate: a transport can retry, a worker can disappear, and an agent can revise its proposal while the authoritative workflow record remains inspectable.
